clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A nurse is preparing to access an implanted venous port for chemotherapy in an outpatient oncology clinic. Which action is appropriate?

options.A: Inspect the port site, cleanse it with an appropriate antiseptic, and access the septum with a non-coring needle.
options.B: Use a standard hypodermic needle because any sterile needle can safely penetrate an implanted port septum.
options.C: Omit skin antisepsis when the port was used earlier that day and the overlying skin appears clean.
options.D: Access the port before inspecting the surrounding chest and neck so manipulation does not affect the assessment.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC's outpatient oncology infection-control plan directs staff to perform hand hygiene and examine the implanted-port site before each access, including the surrounding chest and neck for swelling, erythema, drainage, leakage, pain, discomfort, or tenderness. The port site is then cleansed with an appropriate antiseptic, the portal body stabilized, and the septum accessed with a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle. CDC notes that either clean or sterile gloves may be used for implanted-port access, while some professional-society recommendations add sterile gloves and facemasks; the item therefore does not make one glove type the tested distinction. Option A reflects the core access steps without overstating that glove nuance.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Apply evidence-based implanted-port access steps, including pre-access assessment, skin antisepsis, and use of a non-coring needle.

semantic_correction.source_locator: Section VI.D.1 Implanted Ports — Port Access Procedure: perform hand hygiene; examine site and veins of chest/neck before each access; palpate portal body; perform hand hygiene; wear clean or sterile gloves; cleanse with appropriate antiseptic; stabilize portal body; insert non-coring needle such as a Huber needle until portal backing is felt
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC implanted-port access guidance includes pre-access inspection, antiseptic skin cleansing, and insertion of a non-coring needle; clean or sterile gloves may be used, so a universal sterile-glove requirement should not be inferred from this source.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original correct answer was uniquely longest. The revised item tests only directly supported core port-access steps and preserves CDC's explicit clean-versus-sterile-glove nuance.

option_audit.A: Correct. It combines the CDC-required pre-access inspection, antiseptic cleansing, and non-coring needle use.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC specifically describes use of a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle for implanted-port access.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Skin antisepsis is part of the access procedure and is not omitted because the port was accessed earlier.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. The site and surrounding chest and neck are examined before access rather than after manipulation.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches the CDC implanted-port access sequence without introducing a disputed glove requirement.
cueing_check: All four options are port-access actions of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
